claude.result:
The issue was a classic floating point precision problem. When converting `39.95` dollars to cents by multiplying by 100, JavaScript produces `3995.0000000000005` instead of exactly `3995` due to how binary floating point arithmetic works.

**The fix:** I added `Math.round()` in three places in the money conversion functions:
- **`src/money.js:13`** (parseEuros) — round when parsing decimal amounts 
- **`src/locale.js:18`** (decimalCommaToCents) — round when parsing European comma format
- **`src/money.js:25`** (cellCents) — round when parsing CSV cells

This ensures all price-to-cents conversions produce whole integers, which pass validation. Netflix (€12.99) and Spotify (€10.99) worked fine by chance — most prices avoid the precision trap, but some don't.

All 50 tests pass, and your gym membership at €39.95 now works!
